reason: The sources contain sufficient overlapping facts to support a surprising 45-second story with at least 10 claims.
story: Three hundred million light-years away in the constellation Andromeda, gravity has sculpted two interacting galaxies into a breathtaking cosmic rose. Known as Arp 273, this pair consists of a massive spiral galaxy, UGC 1810, and its smaller companion, UGC 1813. The larger galaxy's disk has been tidally stretched into a flower-like oval by the gravitational pull of the companion below it, which acts as a stem. It is thought that the smaller galaxy has actually passed directly through the larger one. This violent cosmic collision triggered intense star formation, igniting clusters of hot blue stars in the outer arms. Imaged spectacularly by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2010, Arp 273 proves that gravity can paint masterpieces across the universe.
angle: Two colliding galaxies 300 million light-years away have been twisted by gravity into the exact shape of a blooming cosmic rose.

claims.claim: Arp 273 is a pair of interacting galaxies located approximately 300 million light years away.
The pair is located in the constellation Andromeda.
It was compiled in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies by Halton Arp in 1966.
The larger spiral galaxy is known as UGC 1810.
The smaller companion galaxy is known as UGC 1813.
The larger galaxy UGC 1810 is about five times more massive than the smaller galaxy.
The disk of UGC 1810 has been tidally distorted into a flower-like shape by the gravitational pull of UGC 1813.
It is thought that the smaller galaxy has actually passed through the larger one.
One supernova, SN 1962R, has been observed in UGC 1810, discovered on plates taken at the Lick Observatory in December 1962.
SN 1962R had an apparent magnitude of 15.9.
The smaller galaxy shows distinct signs of active star formation at its nucleus.

disputed: S2 notes that Arp 273 was probably discovered by Boris Aleksandrovich Vorontsov-Velyaminov in the 1950s and listed as VV 323, while S1 attributes the initial description to Halton Arp's 1966 atlas. The script should attribute Vorontsov-Velyaminov's finding as an earlier cataloging according to one account.
